name: Olmsted syndrome
aliases: mutilating palmoplantar keratoderma with periorificial keratotic plaques

clinicalPearls: Defined by the combination of a severe, mutilating, bilateral palmoplantar keratoderma with sharply demarcated periorificial keratotic plaques (around the mouth, nose, eyes, anus and genitalia)
The keratoderma is often intensely painful and can be transgredient, with constricting bands and pseudo-ainhum threatening digits
Onset is usually in infancy or early childhood with progressive thickening
Most cases result from dominant gain-of-function mutations in TRPV3, a keratinocyte cation channel; recessive and other genetic forms exist
Associated features may include alopecia, nail dystrophy, oral leucokeratosis and, over time, a risk of squamous cell carcinoma within affected skin
Severe itch, pain and functional disability are prominent and difficult to manage
Management is supportive with emollients/keratolytics, oral retinoids, pain control and surgery for constricting bands; TRPV3-directed and other targeted therapies are under investigation
reference.pathophysiology: Olmsted syndrome is most often caused by dominant gain-of-function mutations in TRPV3, which encodes a transient receptor potential vanilloid cation channel expressed in keratinocytes and involved in temperature sensing, epidermal barrier formation, keratinocyte proliferation and hair growth. Overactivity of the mutant channel increases calcium influx and drives excessive keratinocyte proliferation and abnormal differentiation, together with dysregulated apoptosis and sensory-nerve signalling that generates the marked pain and itch. The result is a severe, mutilating palmoplantar keratoderma with periorificial plaques; chronic hyperproliferation and inflammation also underlie the long-term risk of squamous cell carcinoma. Recessive and phenocopy forms involving other genes have been described.
additionalDifferentials: Pityriasis rubra pilaris with palmoplantar involvement
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing massive orthohyperkeratosis, acanthosis and psoriasiform change
Molecular genetic testing of TRPV3 and related genes
Assessment and monitoring of digital constriction bands and function
Ophthalmological and oral examination for periorificial and mucosal involvement
Surveillance biopsy of chronic or ulcerated plaques for malignant change
redFlags: New, ulcerated or non-healing lesion within keratoderma suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
Uncontrolled pain or itch causing severe disability
Secondary infection of fissured or eroded plaques
reference.prognosis: Olmsted syndrome is a chronic, often progressive and disabling disorder; the keratoderma rarely resolves and can be mutilating, and there is a long-term risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Pain and functional impairment are major and lifelong, though targeted therapies offer emerging hope.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise the diagnostic periorificial plaques and treating as isolated keratoderma
Neglecting early release of constricting bands, risking digital loss
Underestimating pain and itch, which are central to morbidity
Overlooking malignant transformation in long-standing plaques
management: Intensive topical skin care with emollients, keratolytics such as urea or salicylic acid, and mechanical debridement of hyperkeratotic plaques
Oral retinoids such as acitretin as the principal systemic therapy to reduce the keratoderma, with monitoring for retinoid toxicity
Emerging targeted therapy directed at the TRPV3 pathway, including mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus and epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors such as erlotinib in selected cases
Multimodal control of pain and pruritus, incorporating neuropathic analgesics
Prevention and management of digital constriction bands and pseudo-ainhum through physiotherapy, splinting and surgery to preserve the digits
Surveillance for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, with examination and biopsy of chronic or ulcerated plaques
Multidisciplinary dermatology, pain, physiotherapy, ophthalmology and dental care, with genetic counselling for the TRPV3 disorder
